# Base Gaussian localization: exact identities and a depth obstruction

This is a finite-family investigation of base-only Gaussian tilting. The actual continuous fibers remain uniform throughout. The archive search found Gaussian smoothing and hemisphere-transform uses, but no previously saved base Gaussian/Delaunay localization theorem. The results here do not transfer posterior depth to the original measure or prove OC.

## 1. The exact finite posterior family

Let P be a finite lattice-complete base, with positive compatible d-dimensional fibers K_z, d>=1. Put V_z=|K_z|, M=sum V_z and prior pi_z=V_z/M. For a in R^n and t>=0 define

    Z(a,t)=sum_z V_z exp(a.z-t|z|^2/2),
    p_z(a,t)=V_z exp(a.z-t|z|^2/2)/Z(a,t).             (1)

The normalized mixed measure is

    mu_(a,t)=sum_z p_z(a,t) Uniform(K_z).

It is an actual reweighting of the original uniform fibers. It is not asserted to be mixed volume of a new compatible body with masses p_z.

For a fixed bounded statistic g on the original mixed set, let g_z be its average on K_z and G=sum p_z g_z. Write m=sum p_z z and C=Cov_p(z). Direct differentiation gives

    grad_a log Z=m,             Hess_a log Z=C,
    partial_t log Z=-E_p|z|^2/2,
    grad_a G=Cov_p(g_z,z),
    partial_t G=-Cov_p(g_z,|z|^2)/2,
    Hess_a G=E_p[(g_z-G)(z-m)(z-m)^T].                 (2)

In particular

    (partial_t + m.grad_a + (1/2)Delta_a)G=0.           (3)

These formulas apply to every fixed ambient closed cap, including pure-base caps, by setting g_z to its actual fiber capture fraction. Closed boundary mass is retained exactly.

For clarity, the stochastic model that makes G a martingale must be specified. Sample a hidden base Z_0 with law pi and an independent standard Brownian motion B_t, and observe

    A_t=t Z_0+B_t.

Gaussian increment likelihoods show that the conditional law of Z_0 given all observations up to t is exactly p(A_t,t). The endpoint A_t is a sufficient statistic: the log likelihood over any finite time partition sums to A_t.z-t|z|^2/2, and the same assertion follows for the full continuous observation filtration. Conditional on the base, observing A changes nothing about the uniform continuous fiber law.

Consequently each p_z(A_t,t), and every fixed-cap probability, is a bounded martingale. In innovation form

    dA_t=m_t dt+dW_t,
    dp_z=p_z(z-m_t).dW_t,
    dG=Cov_(p_t)(g_z,z).dW_t.                           (4)

Equation (3) also verifies the drift cancellation directly. Driving a_t by Brownian motion WITHOUT the m_t drift under that same probability law does not give the normalized martingales (4); their extra drift is -m.grad_a G. The unnormalized partition function and a change of probability law must not be confused with normalized posterior preservation.

## 2. What fixed centers do preserve

For any fixed actual mark Y let

    D_Y(p)=inf_(closed H containing Y) sum_z p_z g_z(H).

As a function of the finite vector p this is concave and 1-Lipschitz in the l1 norm, being an infimum of linear functions with coefficients in [0,1]. Thus it is measurable without needing any uncountable-family measurability claim. The posterior martingale and conditional Jensen give

    E[D_Y(p_t) | F_s] <= D_Y(p_s),       s<=t.           (5)

Fixed-center depth is a SUPERMARTINGALE. The same conclusion follows directly by comparing with each fixed cap and then taking the infimum at time s. It has the opposite direction from an automatic transfer of posterior lower bounds to a prescribed original center.

The maximal depth D_*(p)=max_(Y in S) D_Y(p) is still 1-Lipschitz in p, but maximization destroys the concavity used in (5). Section 5 gives an actual example in which D_*(p_t) is neither a submartingale nor a supermartingale.

## 3. Terminal parity and a finite-time strengthening

For a deterministic path a_t/t -> c, mass outside

    D_c=argmin_(z in P) |z-c|^2

tends to zero. A closest-point set D_c contains at most one point of each occupied parity. If distinct z,w in it shared a parity, their integer midpoint p would belong to P and

    |p-c|^2=(|z-c|^2+|w-c|^2)/2-|z-w|^2/4

would be strictly smaller. This proof does not need c to be in the interior of the projection. If a_t=tc+b with b fixed, the exact limiting probabilities on D_c are proportional to V_z exp(b.z). For a general o(t) remainder only support containment is asserted.

Actual compatibility gives a useful quantitative identity before the limit. For every anchored relation p=sum_j lambda_j z_j, sum lambda=1, Brunn–Minkowski followed by weighted arithmetic/geometric mean gives

    V_p >= product_j V_(z_j)^(lambda_j).

Hence (1) implies

    p_p / product_j p_(z_j)^(lambda_j)
      =(V_p / product_j V_(z_j)^(lambda_j))
        exp[(t/2)sum_j lambda_j |z_j-p|^2]
      >=exp[(t/2)sum_j lambda_j |z_j-p|^2].              (6)

In particular, for a same-parity pair and its midpoint,

    p_p^2/(p_z p_w)
      =(V_p^2/(V_z V_w))exp[t|z-w|^2/4]
      >=exp[t|z-w|^2/4].                               (7)

In the original integer coordinates, distinct same-parity points have squared distance at least 4. Thus p_z p_w<=exp(-t), since p_p<=1. Select one largest weight in each of the k occupied parity classes. Every unselected weight is at most exp(-t/2): its product with the selected weight in its class is at least its own square. Therefore the selected set has posterior mass at least

    1-(|P|-k)exp(-t/2),                                (8)

uniformly in a. In particular some posterior fiber has weight at least the positive part of (8) divided by k, and its ordinary centroid has posterior mixed depth at least

    (Gamma_d/k)[1-(|P|-k)exp(-t/2)]_+.                  (9)

This is an exact finite-time posterior parity-concentration bound, retaining an actual midpoint volume inequality. It is not an original-measure bound. In the genuine observation process, A_t/t -> Z_0 almost surely; the posterior in fact tends to the single hidden base, rather than necessarily to a multiple-point Delaunay cell.

## 4. Exact all-normal depth on a three-fiber product

Take n=d=1,

    P={-1,0,1},       K_z=[-1,1],
    C=[-1,1] times [-1,1].

This is an actual complete convex family. Its original total mass is 6, original normalized base weights are 1/3, and k(P)=2. Let arbitrary positive posterior weights be p_-,p_0,p_+, summing to one.

At each endpoint base, the fiber center has depth p_-/2 or p_+/2, respectively. Its own interval gives the lower bound for every containing cap; a finite sufficiently steep base tilt isolates its own half interval and attains it. The same isolation shows that the center is the unique maximizer of depth within either endpoint fiber.

At the middle mark (0,0), any nonvertical normal can be normalized by reflection to the cut X+a z>=0. The own capture is p_0/2. The two endpoint fractions are F(a) and F(-a)=1-F(a), where

    F(a)=min(1,max(0,(1+a)/2)).

As a ranges over R, F ranges over [0,1]. Their least weighted sum is therefore min(p_-,p_+). Pure-base cuts have mass p_0+p_- or p_0+p_+, which cannot lower this value. Hence

    D_((0,0))(p)=p_0/2+min(p_-,p_+).                   (10)

Continuous reflection X->-X preserves the entire posterior measure. Halfspace-depth superlevels are convex, so the middle-fiber maximum occurs at X=0. Thus the exact GLOBAL depth, with all marks and normals included, is

    D_*(p)=max{p_-/2,p_+/2,p_0/2+min(p_-,p_+)}.         (11)

Equivalently, putting R=p_-+p_+ and D=p_+-p_-,

    D_*(p)=1/2-|D|/2+(R+3|D|-2)_+/4.                  (12)

The original measure has D_*=1/2 at the middle mark, while either endpoint center has original depth 1/6.

## 5. Maximal posterior depth has neither martingale direction

For the Gaussian posterior of this uniform product,

    (p_-,p_0,p_+)
      =(e^(-a-t/2),1,e^(a-t/2))/(1+2e^(-t/2)cosh a).   (13)

At t=0,a=0, equation (11) gives D_*=1/2. At every finite t>0 all three posterior weights are strictly positive. If a!=0 then p_-!=p_+, so all three entries in the maximum (11) are STRICTLY below 1/2. Under the genuine observation law A_t has a continuous Gaussian-mixture density, hence A_t!=0 almost surely. Therefore

    E D_*(p_t)<1/2=D_*(p_0)     for every finite t>0.   (14)

This rules out the submartingale assertion. On the other hand p_t tends almost surely to delta_(Z_0), and (11) tends to 1/2. Bounded convergence gives E D_*(p_t)->1/2. A supermartingale cannot have expectation strictly below 1/2 at a finite time and later converge in expectation to 1/2. Thus it is not a supermartingale either.

The failure occurs for actual best posterior centers, not merely a centroid-selection heuristic.

## 6. A finite exact posterior winner fails the original target

Set

    t=2 log 2,          a=log 8.

The exact weights in (13) are

    (p_-,p_0,p_+)=(1,16,64)/81.

The middle maximum is 1/9, the negative endpoint maximum is 1/162, and the positive endpoint maximum is 32/81. Thus the UNIQUE posterior deepest mark is (1,0). Its posterior depth exceeds Gamma_1/k=1/4, but its ORIGINAL depth is

    1/6 < 1/4.                                         (15)

The same strict winner persists for an open interval of a around log 8, which has positive probability at this finite observation time. At the limiting posterior, with original probability 2/3 the hidden base is an endpoint; eventually (11) selects that endpoint, and its original center still has depth 1/6. Thus a good posterior center does not become a valid original center almost surely.

The original body is not an OC counterexample: its middle point has original depth 1/2. The examples refute the simple posterior-depth martingale and posterior-winner transfer principles. Any localization proof would need a further invariant retaining the original cap constraints at a single actual mark; fixed-cap martingales, terminal parity, and posterior heavy-fiber bounds alone do not provide it.
